Nvidia's effective monopoly over the most powerful chips has made U.S. export controls a key tool in Washington's effort to preserve its advantage over China in the AI race. American AI labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic are locked in a training and pricing battle with Chinese developers, including Moonshot AI, which makes the Kimi family of models. Moonshot was looking to lease capacity powered by Nvidia's Blackwell systems, advanced chips currently subject to those export controls which effectively ban their import into China, three of the sources told CNBC. In July, the White House said the Chinese AI lab had accessed Nvidia's Blackwell chips via a facility in Thailand. U.S. export controls restrict the shipment of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China, but remote access via overseas data centers offers a loophole. Current law does not give regulators broad authority to control companies' access to those chips through cloud services hosted overseas. Moonshot, Nvidia, the White House, the U.S. Department of Commerce, China's embassy in the U.K. and its Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not respond to a request for comment. One of the sources said they were also aware of interest in clusters for training. Talks for arrangements that would see Moonshot rent access to clusters of 8,000 or more Blackwell GPUs hosted in the region have taken place, one source said. They described the Chinese AI lab as "very aggressive" in its pursuit of more computing power. One of the sources told CNBC that talks on securing Moonshot compute in Europe had taken place since the White House said it had done so via Thailand. Moonshot did not comment at the time. Racing to secure computing power Founded in 2023, Beijing-based Moonshot AI is one of China's leading model builders. It released a new model in July that Moonshot said closed the gap with leading systems built by Anthropic and OpenAI. The model saw significant uptake as a cheaper alternative to U.S. offerings. Around the time Kimi K3 was released, Moonshot said demand had stretched its capacity, and it temporarily paused new subscriptions to prioritize compute for current members. "We're adding capacity as fast as we can and will reopen new subscription spots in batches," the company said in a LinkedIn post. Leasing AI compute is a booming industry, with customers, or offtakers, typically taking capacity for a fee and paying an upfront cost to secure the deal, which is a percentage of the lifetime contract value. One source said it had been proposed that Moonshot pay 30% to 50% more upfront than a non-Chinese offtaker would. Arrangements with Chinese customers can be more lucrative upfront, as neoclouds and financing firms look to hedge against a potential future ban of remote access agreements. Management also reaffirmed the company's full-year 2026 revenue guidance of $1.6 billion to $1.7 billion. Peloton Interactive — The maker of fitness equipment jumped 7% after Peloton Interactive posted fiscal first-quarter revenue of $559 million, besting the LSEG consensus estimate of $554 million. However, earnings of 19 cents per share missed the 21 cents expected. Wendy's — Shares were little changed after the fast food chain rejected a $1.4 billion takeover offer from a Trian Fund Management-led group. The group late last month offered $7.35 per share in cash to take Wendy's private. Unity Software — Shares of the game development company surged 22% following blowout results. Unity Software posted third-quarter earnings of 25 cents per share on revenue of $622 million. Analysts surveyed by LSEG had expected per-share earnings of 5 cents on revenue of $567 million. Qualcomm — The chipmaker plunged 9% even after posting a slight earnings beat in its fiscal fourth-quarter financial report . Qualcomm sees adjusted earnings of $2.15 to $2.35 per share in the current quarter, while analysts polled by FactSet were seeking $2.26 per share. AppLovin — Shares rallied 19% following stronger-than-expected third-quarter results. The software company known for mobile game advertising posted adjusted EBITDA of $1.84 billion, more than the FactSet $1.73 billion consensus estimate. Revenue of $2.18 billion exceeded the forecast of $2.07 billion. Expedia — The online booking company slid more than 6% after Expedia issued mostly weaker-than-expected guidance for the current quarter. It sees revenue between $3.69 billion and $3.75 billion in the fourth quarter, but analysts polled by FactSet on average expected $3.74 billion. Coherent — The optical materials company dipped 2% though it posted earnings and revenue that topped estimates. Adjusted earnings of $2.09 per share topped the $1.99 per share consensus estimate from FactSet. Revenue also came in above estimates, as did guidance for the current quarter. Zillow — Shares sank about 15% after the company missed on key metrics in its third-quarter earnings report. Adjusted earnings came in at 55 cents per share, compared with the 59 cents per share expected by LSEG. Revenue also was weaker than expected, at $724 million compared to expectations for $754 million. Klaviyo – The maker of the customer relationship management platform slid about 5% even as the company reported stronger than expected third-quarter results. Klaviyo posted adjusted earnings of 22 cents per share on revenue of $387.2 million, while the consensus called for 17 cents per share and $380 million, according to FactSet. Klaviyo also lifted its full-year revenue guidance. MercadoLibre – Shares slid 6% following third-quarter earnings that missed estimates. The e-commerce platform earned $8.83 per share, compared to the FactSet consensus estimate of $9.27 a share. However, revenue of $10.75 billion beat the expectation for $10.69 billion. Arm Holdings — The designer of central processing units dropped more than 5% even after a strong earnings report. The UK-based company reported adjusted earnings of 52 cents per share, besting the LSEG consensus estimate of 47 cents. Cava — The restaurant chain tumbled more than 8% after it reported third-quarter results that missed expectations. Earnings of 11 cents a share disappointed the LSEG consensus estimate for 12 cents. Cava posted revenue of $356 million, while analysts expected the number to be $359 million. Wolfspeed – The semiconductor manufacturer fell more than 3% after posting a wider-than-expected loss in the fiscal first quarter. Wolfspeed's adjusted loss of $2.03 per share came in worse than the FactSet consensus estimate for a $1.99 per share loss. Figma — The software stock dropped almost 7% even after the cloud-based design platform posted third-quarter results that bested expectations. Figma posted adjusted earnings of 10 cents a share on revenue of $391 million, while the LSEG consensus called for 5 cents a share and $376 million. HubSpot – Shares of the customer platform company slid 9% following disappointing fourth-quarter earnings and revenue guidance. HubSpot expects to earn between $3.85 and $3.87 per share on revenue of $945 million to $947 million.
